name: Antia-Buch helical advancement

card.summary: A reconstructive ear surgery technique that slides ear rim tissue forward to close a defect in the helix, preserving the ear's outline and a natural look.
card.aka: Helical rim advancement flap, chondrocutaneous helical rim advancement
card.note: A surgical procedure performed by dermatologic, plastic or ENT surgeons; most literature concerns skin-cancer defects.

quick.overview:
The Antia-Buch flap is a surgical way to close a gap in the rim of the ear, the helix. Surgeons free the rim along with the attached skin and cartilage and slide it forward to cover the defect, keeping the ear's curve.

It matters for appearance because it repairs ear defects, such as those left after skin-cancer removal, while keeping the ear looking natural. Surgeons have also used variants to reduce oversized ears and to repair keloid sites on the rim.
quick.how: It is done in surgery under local or general anaesthesia. Incisions run from the defect down toward the earlobe and sometimes up along the groove behind the rim, and the freed tissue is advanced and stitched. Healing is followed in clinic visits.
quick.risks: Reported complications include hematoma, which occurred in two of 47 patients in one series, and, with some designs, ear shortening or cupping. Complications are discussed with the surgeon.

lead: The Antia-Buch flap, or chondrocutaneous helical rim advancement flap, is a reconstructive technique named after the surgeons N. H. Antia and V. I. Buch. It closes defects of the helix, the outer rim of the ear, by advancing the rim tissue (skin and cartilage together) along its own length [1][2].

It matters for looks because the rim defines the ear's outline. A defect there can be closed with a straight wedge excision, which tends to leave the ear cupped, or with an advancement flap, which keeps the curve [3]. About 2-4% of skin cancers occur on the helix, so most reports come from dermatologic surgery [1].

In aesthetics communities, the technique appears in discussion of ear surgery. Plastic surgeons have described double helical rim advancement flaps with scaphal resection as a way to reduce large ears (macrotia) and reconstruct rim defects [4].

chain: Defect or oversized rim is addressed
Rim tissue is advanced and sutured
Ear outline preserved with a smaller or repaired rim
angle.text: Surgeons use the technique to repair rim defects while keeping the ear's natural shape, and a double-flap variant can make large ears smaller.

infobox: Rim defect closure, ear reduction, keloid recurrence

paras: Incisions run from the defect down into the lobule and, when needed, up along the helical sulcus into the helical crus. The skin behind the ear is undermined widely so that the resulting well-vascularised flap can move [1]. Central cartilage may be trimmed to relieve tension [3].

Reconstruction of helical rim defects after skin-cancer removal is the main use; if the cartilage is intact and the defect is central, other closures may be preferred, while rim defects are often treated with a helical rim advancement flap [3].

A variant with double flaps and scaphal resection has been described for macrotia and rim defects [4]. A case series reported that rim advancement after helical keloid excision was used to try to reduce recurrences [5].

A 1995 report of 47 patients described no ischemic necrosis, two hematomas that healed after drainage, and favourable cosmetic results [1]. A cadaver study with 10 patient results examined how rim advancement affects ear length and cupping and closure tension [2]. Case series describe the double-flap variant and the keloid application [4][5].
Reported issues include hematoma [1] and reduction in ear length or cupping depending on technique [2].

timeline.event: Report of 47 patients treated with the Antia-Buch flap [1].
Biomechanics of the flap studied in cadaver ears [2].
Double helical rim advancement flaps for ear reduction and reconstruction reviewed [4].
